newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco lawyer Woody Wilner: a man with a mission.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco lawyer Woody Wilner: a man with a mission.

text.p: Norwood "Woody" Wilner is a man with a vocation: playing David to the Goliath tobacco companies of the United States.

"I think I was put on Earth to do this," Wilner said as he prepared for jury selection Monday in a wrongful death lawsuit in which he will take on R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., America's second-biggest cigarette maker.
The case, known as Raulerson vs. R.J. Reynolds, is very simple, Wilner said. He contends that Reynolds knew it was peddling a deadly product but continued to hype it as pleasurable and safe.
As a result, Jean Connor, who smoked at least a pack of Reynolds' Salem cigarettes each day for years, died of lung cancer in 1995 at age 49, he says.
Wilner represents her estate, handled by her sister, Dana Raulerson, and the interests of her three grown children.
Reynolds lawyers are expected to argue that Connor was not an addict but someone who admitted that she liked to smoke.
The defence also will present witnesses to testify that Connor's cancer cannot conclusively be linked to her smoking.
Daniel Donahue, Reynolds' senior vice-president, predicted that jurors will not be affected by "a flamboyant lawyer who likes the publicity." R.J. Reynolds is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.

Wilner, 48, is a blunt, unassuming figure who works at a small Jacksonville law firm. Yet he has launched one of the most formidable legal assaults ever on the tobacco industry, filing 300 to 400 lawsuits on behalf of smokers and their families.
And he has won, at least once.

Last summer Wilner won a watershed $750,000 judgment for his clients, ex-smoker Grady Carter and his wife, Millie, shaking tobacco firms on Wall Street and encouraging anti-smoking activists across the country.
The award against defendant Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., a unit of Britain's B.A.T Industries Plc, was the largest verdict to date in tobacco liability litigation. The B.A.T unit has appealed.
Asked what will be different this time as he takes on Reynolds, Wilner grinned and said, "If we have our druthers, nothing."
Eschewing high-tech presentation aids in favour of an overhead projector and stacks of transparencies, Wilner can cut a less than inspiring figure in the courtroom at first glance.
In the Carter trial he shuffled papers and interrupted himself to start a new thought, only to interrupt himself again, and many analysts figured he didn't stand a chance.
"We all underestimated Woody," analyst Gary Black of Bernstein Research in New York told the Florida Times-Union.

Wilner himself refuses to speculate on the meaning of another win against the tobacco industry. A verdict in his client's favour means just one thing, he said: "Appeal. They'll file an appeal and send out a bunch of press releases."
